img_6205c940ef544e0b.original_title: Francis Marion Dowling Sr And Iola Stower Dowling
img_6205c940ef544e0b.description: Color studio portrait of an elderly couple: Francis Marion Dowling Sr. (b. April 9, 1892, Bethany, Brooke County, West Virginia; d. February 17, 1979, Riverside County, CA) in a light suit and browline glasses, and his wife Iola May (Stower) Dowling (b. September 3, 1898; d. June 30, 1982) in a lace dress with pearl necklace and earrings. The couple married May 25, 1924 in Glendora, CA, and later settled in Beaumont, where Francis Sr. and his son Francis Jr. planted some 25,000 fruit trees, the start of the Dowling Fruit Orchard on Highway 60 (fruit stand opened 1952, operated until 2021). Both appear to be in their mid-70s to 80s, and the color print, his browline glasses, and her dress style all point to the late 1960s-1970s; the photo must predate his death in February 1979. The print shows heavy red/magenta dye shift typical of aging chromogenic prints of that era. The catalog's former date of c. 1900-1920 was impossible given the sitters' ages and color photography.

img_9299c7a090b03878.description: Sepia studio portrait of Francis Marion Dowling Sr. (b. April 9, 1892, Bethany, Brooke County, West Virginia; d. February 17, 1979, Riverside County, CA) as a young man, head-and-shoulders in a dark jacket, tall stiff white collar, and light four-in-hand tie with a stickpin visible below the knot. Dowling married Iola May Stower in Glendora in 1924 and later farmed in Beaumont, where he and his son Francis Jr. planted some 25,000 fruit trees, the origin of the Dowling Fruit Orchard on Highway 60. His birthplace makes it likely this portrait was taken before or during his migration west, so a West Virginia or Midwest studio is possible.

img_ed9a0626308ebccf.title: Francis Dowling Sr. with Golden State Cherry Orchard truck
img_ed9a0626308ebccf.original_title: Francis Dowling Sr With Golden State Orchard Truck
img_ed9a0626308ebccf.description: A man identified by the family as Francis Marion Dowling Sr. (1892-1979), in work shirt, trousers, and a brimmed hat, stands beside an early Ford Model T cut down into a flatbed farm truck, gesturing toward its open cab; a placard wired to the stake bed reads 'GOLDEN STATE CHERRY ORCHARD' with a third, illegible smaller line beneath. Behind the truck is a flat-roofed adobe- or plaster-walled building, and orchard branches overhang the frame at left. The wooden-spoke wheels, brass-era body remnants, and runabout-to-truck conversion are typical of working Model Ts in the late 1910s and 1920s, consistent with the catalog's c. 1918-1925 range, when Dowling Sr. was in his late twenties to early thirties. The San Gorgonio Pass was a noted cherry district — Cherry Valley's commercial orchards date from the early 1900s and Beaumont's Cherry Festival began in the 1910s — but no business called 'Golden State Cherry Orchard' could be located in accessible sources, and the family's documented Beaumont orchard on Highway 60 was planted a generation later (early 1950s), so this photograph records an earlier chapter of the family's fruit-growing life whose location is unconfirmed. Note that the sign reads 'Cherry Orchard,' not 'Orchard' as in the old catalog title.

img_fe6493dfb389b7f5.title: Francis Marion Dowling Jr. and Estella Dowling on a porch
img_fe6493dfb389b7f5.description: Black-and-white snapshot of Francis Marion Dowling Jr. (b. February 13, 1925; d. October 8, 2016) in a light suit and dark tie standing hand-in-hand with his wife Estella, who wears a light knee-length dress, on the porch of a single-story house with large multi-pane windows, flanking shrubs in the foreground. Dowling Jr. — Beaumont Schools valedictorian, a Navy electronics technician in World War II, and a 1950 UCLA horticulture graduate — bought land on Highway 60 in Beaumont where he and his father planted some 25,000 fruit trees; the family's Dowling Fruit Orchard stand (opened 1952, 'Since 1954' on its sign) became a Pass landmark until it closed in November 2021. He appears here in his mid-twenties to early thirties, which with the couple's postwar clothing dates the photograph to roughly 1948-1958 — the catalog's former 1930-1945 range is impossible, as Dowling Jr. was born in 1925 and is plainly an adult here. Estella predeceased her husband; the couple's children were John, Lynette, and Janet.

img_57a9c9df6e55e692.description: Black-and-white photograph of two men in plaid work shirts and brimmed hats posing in a field of grass and low hills with a shield-and-eagle 'FARM BUREAU MEMBER' sign mounted on a metal fence post between them: at right the elder Francis Marion Dowling Sr. (1892-1979), in browline glasses and pleated khakis, grips the post; at left his son Francis Marion Dowling Jr. (1925-2016) steadies the sign. Father and son planted some 25,000 fruit trees on Dowling Jr.'s Highway 60 land in Beaumont after his 1950 UCLA horticulture degree, building the ranch behind the Dowling Fruit Orchard stand (opened 1952), and the membership sign presumably marks that ranch's enrollment in the Farm Bureau. Sr. appears in his late sixties to seventies and Jr. in his thirties to early forties, which with Sr.'s browline glasses (a post-1947 style) and the ranch's early-1950s founding dates the photograph to roughly 1955-1972. The catalog's former 1930-1945 range is impossible: Jr. was a schoolboy then, and both men here are clearly older. The filename's 'cropped' indicates this scan was trimmed from a larger print.

img_a6ec55f14a4d13dc.description: A color print showing Dowling Fruit Orchard founder Francis Marion Dowling Jr. (1925-2016) in a red plaid jacket, wheeling stacked cartons labeled 'Cherries' on a tall wooden-framed hand truck (called a 'clamp truck' in the collection filename) through the doorway of his Beaumont stand, with jam shelves, cooler doors, and hand-lettered 'No shirts, no service' and 'No pets allowed in store' signs behind him. Dowling, a Beaumont High valedictorian and WWII Navy electronics technician, earned a horticulture degree at UCLA in 1950, bought land on US Highway 60, planted some 25,000 fruit trees with his father Francis Sr., and opened the roadside store in 1952. Cherry season was his favorite time of year, and he was named honored citizen of Beaumont's 1993 Cherry Festival. His evident age here (late 80s) places the photo in roughly the last decade of his life; the file's 2022 EXIF timestamp is a Windows Photo Editor digitization date, not the capture date.

img_1ad76840ab48ba0e.title: John Dowling in the packing barn, Dowling Fruit Orchard, November 2021
img_1ad76840ab48ba0e.description: Digital photograph of John Dowling, son of founder Francis Dowling Jr., standing among retired ranch equipment in the old packing barn at Dowling Fruit Orchard, wearing a shirt embroidered with the store's logo. EXIF data shows it was taken with an Apple iPhone 7 on November 19, 2021 at 11:51 a.m. — days before the stand closed for good at the end of that month, and one day before the Record-Gazette published its closure story. John (59 at closing, so born c. 1962) had worked the stand full-time since 1989 and ran it with his wife Shelly in its final years, when the property had diminished from 62 to about 31 acres. This is not one of the Record-Gazette's photos (those were credited to writer David James Heiss and show different scenes); it comes from the same iPhone 7 that shot this collection's storefront-banners photo later the same day, evidently a private documentation visit during the stand's final weeks.

img_2eee4fa95a275d4d.description: Smartphone photograph of the Dowling Fruit Orchard storefront at 38021 US Highway 60, Beaumont, under its rooftop 'FARM FRESH PRODUCE' and 'DRIED FRUIT NUTS CANDY' sign boards, with hand-painted fluorescent banners for persimmons, plums (99 cents), 'Sweet Red Pomegrantes 99c lb' (sic), fresh strawberries, and a wild-game-jerky placard, plus orange shopping carts out front. EXIF data dates it to November 19, 2021 at 12:56 p.m. — the same iPhone 7 documentation visit that produced this collection's John Dowling portrait — in the last month before the stand, opened by Francis Dowling in 1952 amid 62 acres of orchards, closed at the end of November 2021. The pomegranate and persimmon banners mark late-fall harvest at the stand, which grew both crops on the property. The site was sold, a business liquidation sale began December 9, 2021, and the parcel was subsequently proposed for the 610,000-square-foot Orchard Logistics warehouse.

img_dc9b98dd0bb1264f.title: Dowling Fruit Orchard stand on Highway 60, c. 1950s-1960s
img_dc9b98dd0bb1264f.description: The only period photograph in the catalog's Dowling group: a black-and-white view of the roadside stand on US Highway 60 east of Beaumont, its roofline carrying open skeleton-letter signs reading 'DOWLING FRUIT ORCHARD' over a band of boards advertising 'DRIED FRUIT — DATES — EGGS — NU[TS]', with a hand-painted 'Tomatoes' sign at the unpaved drive entrance and shaded produce tables under the canopy. Francis Dowling opened the store in 1952, when 62 surrounding acres produced persimmons, jujubes, pomegranates, quince, cherries, peaches, plums, figs and apricots; the 'Dates Eggs' sign wording here differs from the 'DRIED FRUIT NUTS CANDY' boards documented in November 2021, consistent with an early view of the stand. The catalog copy is only a 462x338 web-resolution file re-saved December 1, 2021 — days after the stand closed — and the original print has not been located; the San Gorgonio Pass Historical Society circulated a vintage view of the stand in July 2020 credited 'courtesy of Flickr and the Downey Conservancy', a possible source trail.

The misspelled, hand-lettered sign typifies the folk signage that made the stand a Highway 60 landmark.

img_1ac667107bd74996.title: Beaumont Fire Department Uniforms on Exhibit (2021 photo)
img_1ac667107bd74996.original_title: City Of Beaumont Work And Dress Uniforms
img_1ac667107bd74996.description: A modern color photograph (iPhone 7, March 27, 2021 per EXIF) of a museum-style display of City of Beaumont Fire Department uniforms, with an unidentified man — plausibly a retired Beaumont firefighter or the uniforms' donor — posing beside it. The display holds a khaki short-sleeve work uniform with badge and Beaumont shoulder patch, a navy dress uniform with peaked cap, badge, and 'Beaumont Fire' shoulder patch on a mannequin, a yellow wildland jacket at left, and a brass nozzle at the base, all set against an enlarged black-and-white photograph of firefighters at work. The uniforms date from the municipal fire department era, which ended when the City Council voted in November 1978 to contract fire protection to the California Department of Forestry — documented by a Record-Gazette 11-28-78 clipping in the same source folder and by the city's official statement that it has contracted with Riverside County Fire/CAL FIRE 'since 1978.' The exhibit venue is unconfirmed; the interior shows a tiled floor, wood-and-glass double doors, and an antique stove. The khaki shirt and badge in this display also appear in a separate November 2020 close-up photo in this collection (img_0f63f186060123e4), taken with the same iPhone 7.

img_865e3dceea5cb7ba.title: Beaumont FD Parade Engine 'Engine Co. No. 2' in the Cherry Festival Parade, late 1970s
img_865e3dceea5cb7ba.original_title: Beaumont Fire Department Vintage Lafrance Fire Engine In Cherry Festival Parade Late 1970S
img_865e3dceea5cb7ba.description: A firefighter in black helmet and red suspenders sits at the wheel of the Beaumont Fire Department's white open-cab antique pumper, gold-lettered 'BEAUMONT FIRE DEPARTMENT / ENGINE CO. No. 2,' with a hose reel mounted behind the cab and ground ladders alongside — rolling in Beaumont's annual Cherry Festival parade, annotated late 1970s. The same engine, identified in the department archive as a LaFrance kept for parade duty, appears parked at the Maple Avenue fire station in a 1971 archive photo in this collection ('...LaFrance fire engine used for parades... dated 1971'), so the make rests on that annotation rather than on visible markings. The Cherry Festival began in 1918 and its parade is documented from 1919 (a Calisphere item titled 'The Cherry Festival Parade, 1919' survives in the Beaumont Library District collection); the festival celebrated its 100th anniversary in 2018. A late-1970s date would place this appearance at the very end of the municipal department, which passed to CDF/Riverside County in 1978. The digital file is itself an iPhone re-photograph (June 11, 2023 per EXIF) of a silk-finish color print, whose stock is consistent with the 1970s.

img_5b02c2385f9cb46d.original_title: Beaumont Volunteer Fire Department Car Plate From 1970S
img_5b02c2385f9cb46d.description: A modern photograph (iPhone 7, November 24, 2020 per EXIF) of a red license-plate-sized courtesy plate reading 'MEMBER / FIRE DEPT / BEAUMONT, CALIFORNIA' in white and black, with four mounting slots and a white border. Plates like this were carried on volunteer firefighters' personal vehicles to identify members responding to alarms — Beaumont's department relied on volunteers through its final municipal decades, as sibling photos in this collection ('Beaumont City Volunteer Fire Department 1973') attest. The collection annotation dates the plate to the 1970s, the department's last decade before the city contracted fire protection to CDF/Riverside County in 1978; the plate's exact manufacture date is unverified. The photograph was taken two days before the badge photo in this collection, with the same iPhone 7 — evidently one session documenting Beaumont fire memorabilia.

img_6f617c49fb8ae29d.title: City of Beaumont Fire Dept. GMC Pumper at a Grass Fire, c. 1963-1978
img_6f617c49fb8ae29d.description: A red pumper on an early-1950s GMC conventional chassis stands in dry grass with smoke rising behind it — working a grass fire. The door reads 'CITY OF BEAUMONT FIRE DEPT.' around the city seal, which carries Beaumont's incorporation date, 'Inc. Nov. 18, 1912.' The truck wears a black California exempt plate ('E' octagon, 72587); black-base plates were first issued in 1963, so the photograph cannot predate 1963, and the municipal department ceased operations when the city contracted to CDF/Riverside County in 1978 — the collection annotation says 1970s. The front bumper stencil reads '1794'; the filename's 'Engine 24' designation cannot be confirmed from the image. The same pumper appears in two other photos in this collection: at the department's earlier 500 Grace Avenue station and parked in the right bay of the new Maple Avenue station in a 1971 archive photo, showing a service life spanning both station eras. The file is a February 10, 2009 flatbed scan (HP psc2400) of a color print, made in the same session as the 1972 group photo scan.

img_b690890e951ac18c.title: Beaumont Fire Department at the Maple Avenue Station, 1972
img_b690890e951ac18c.description: Eight men of the Beaumont Fire Department line up before the open apparatus bay of their station in 1972 — seven in khaki uniform shirts with shoulder patches (the second man from left wears a tie, possibly the chief), one at right in civilian sweater, with an engine's beacon and speaker visible in the bay behind them. The building's diamond-pattern concrete block and decorative screen-block match the fire station built on Maple Avenue in 1969 (its construction was covered in the Record-Gazette of March 21, 1969 — clippings in this same source folder) and the station shown in the Beaumont Library District's 1971 photographs on Calisphere; the building serves today as Riverside County Fire Station 66, 628 Maple Avenue. In 1972 Beaumont still ran its own combination paid-and-volunteer department; six years later, on November 28, 1978, the Record-Gazette reported the City Council's vote to contract fire services to the California Department of Forestry, and the city has been served by CDF/Riverside County Fire since 1978. The chief at the time was likely Mickey Wright, named to the post in October 1967 after Clarence 'Pappy' Lewis retired, per a Record-Gazette clipping of April 30, 1968 in this collection. The file is a February 10, 2009 flatbed scan of a black-and-white print.

img_f03f7f375191edf6.title: Beaumont Fire Department hose cart displayed at the fire station, 628 Maple Avenue
img_f03f7f375191edf6.description: A black-and-white print of the Beaumont Fire Department's antique hand-drawn hose cart, loaded with rolled hose and carrying a painted 'BEAUMONT FIRE DEPT' sign, displayed on the lawn of the city fire station at 628 Maple Avenue — the street number '628' visible over the garage matches the address on the department's 1977 letterhead elsewhere in this collection, and the building still serves as Riverside County Fire Station 66. A square-body GMC fire engine (a cab style introduced in 1973) stands in the open apparatus bay at right, consistent with the catalog's 1973–1980 range; the cart was evidently preserved as a relic of the department's early hand-drawn era, the same era invoked by the horse-drawn wagon emblem on the department letterhead. The scan's filename records that it was downloaded from Calisphere, and Google's index of the Beaumont Library District's Calisphere collection lists an item titled 'Front of Beaumont Fire Dept located at 628 Maple Ave, Firestation #66' — the probable source, though the item page could not be fetched to confirm (Calisphere blocks automated access). Beaumont ran its own city fire department until December 1, 1978, when the council contracted fire services to the California Division of Forestry; the city has contracted with CDF (now CAL FIRE)/Riverside County Fire ever since.

img_530924ee0ded82c6.title: City of Beaumont Fire Department letter to Emma Estrada, May 26, 1977
img_530924ee0ded82c6.description: A typed letter on City of Beaumont Fire Department letterhead — 628 Maple Avenue, Michael C. Diebner, Fire Chief, with a red emblem of a horse-drawn fire wagon — dated May 26, 1977 and addressed to Emma Estrada at 218 'B' Street, Beaumont. It confirms that the department's rescue unit responded to her address that day 'as a public service without charge,' warns that other agencies may bill for similar services, and invites her to call again at need; it is signed by John McLaughlin, Engineer, on the chief's behalf. McLaughlin is corroborated as a Beaumont FD member by a 1976 photo with fireman Scott DeForge in this same collection folder, and Diebner is the chief who eighteen months later presented the CDF contract that ended the city-run department (Record-Gazette, Nov. 28, 1978, also in this catalog). The letter is a small primary document of the city-run department's final years — free rescue service was one of the points argued when the council voted to contract fire services to the state in 1978 — and it reached the collection through the Estrada family, whose materials appear throughout this catalog.

img_a48b18e93521487b.title: Record-Gazette front page: 'Council Votes To Contract Fire Services With CDF', November 28, 1978
img_a48b18e93521487b.original_title: Council Votes To Contract Fire Services With Cdf News Clip From Record Gazette
img_a48b18e93521487b.description: Front page of the Record-Gazette (Banning; masthead: 'The Community Voice of the San Gorgonio Pass Since 1908'), 70th year, No. 232, Tuesday, November 28, 1978, carrying Jim Lyntton's report 'Council Votes To Contract Fire Services With CDF.' The Beaumont City Council, rejecting a citizens' 'S.O.S.' (Save Our Services) campaign, voted 4–1 — Councilman J.E. 'Duke' DeForge dissenting — to contract city fire services to the California Division of Forestry beginning December 1, 1978, at an estimated $102,016 a year including $64,068 in salaries. Fire Chief Michael Diebner presented a line-by-line explanation of the contract; city firefighters were approved for transfer to CDF with raises (including fireman Scott DeForge), the fire house was to be leased to the county for $3 a year, and City Manager Glenn Sparks and citizens debated liability coverage and Proposition 13's toll on the city budget. The page marks the end of Beaumont's city-run fire department: the city's own website confirms it has contracted with CDF (now CAL FIRE)/Riverside County Fire ever since. The Record-Gazette's 1968–1993 run is digitized in the California Digital Newspaper Collection at UC Riverside, where this issue should be verifiable.
img_a48b18e93521487b.rights: Rule 5 (named newspaper clipping 1931+): Record-Gazette (Banning, CA), published November 28, 1978 — still within copyright term. Contact the Record-Gazette, Banning, CA, for reproduction rights; the digitized run at CDNC (UC Riverside) provides research access, not republication rights.

img_97db6b297170b04e.original_title: Beaumont Fire Department Public Safety Demonstration Engineer John Mclaughlin With Bullhorn Early 1980S
img_97db6b297170b04e.description: A color snapshot of a public fire-safety demonstration on a grass field: a firefighter in a yellow jacket — identified by the collection filename as Engineer John McLaughlin — narrates through a bullhorn beside staged household props, including an electric range, a plywood panel fitted with a curtained window, a mattress, and upholstered furniture, with a fire extinguisher standing by; children watch from the foreground. The props are the classic set pieces of a home-hazard demonstration (kitchen, curtain, and bedding fires) of the kind fire departments staged for schools and Fire Prevention Week audiences. McLaughlin is documented in this collection as a Beaumont Fire Department engineer — he signed the department's May 26, 1977 letter to Emma Estrada and appears in a 1976 photo with fireman Scott DeForge — and after December 1978 Beaumont's fire protection was run under contract by CDF/Riverside County, so an early-1980s demonstration would have been under that arrangement. The catalog had flattened the folder's 'early 1980s' descriptor to an exact 1980; the date is restored here as a 1980–1984 range.

img_d94679a3a45f55c0.title: Eucalyptus trees on Beaumont Avenue — Beaumont Land and Water Company print, c. 1905–1912
img_d94679a3a45f55c0.description: A mounted photographic print looking along unpaved Beaumont Avenue: a double row of tall eucalyptus at left, fenced fields, utility poles, a horse-drawn buggy in the roadway, and a farmhouse among younger trees at right. The print carries a typed label 'BEAUMONT AVE', a purple rubber stamp reading 'BEAUMONT LAND AND WATER COMPANY', and 'Beaumont Ave' in ink along the bottom margin. The Beaumont Land and Water Company was incorporated at Riverside in mid-August 1907 (Riverside Enterprise and San Bernardino Sun, Aug. 17, 1907) under president Clarendon B. Eyer, and per the Los Angeles Herald of Aug. 18, 1909 it purchased the Beaumont hotel, townsite, lands and water in August 1907 from the San Francisco bank that had held them since the 1890s foreclosure, then promoted the town aggressively from Los Angeles offices. The company stamp therefore places this print in that promotional era, and the timeline's 'c. 1900' date was an unsourced AI estimate. A caveat: an earlier 'Beaumont Land and Water company' appears in an 1894 Riverside Enterprise item, so a 1890s stamp cannot be absolutely excluded, but the typed office label and the 1907–08 promotion campaign make the later era far more likely.
img_d94679a3a45f55c0.rights: Anonymous promotional photograph, c. 1905–1912. Likely out of copyright (anonymous unpublished works run 120 years from creation, and earlier expiry applies if the Beaumont Land and Water Co. published it in pre-1931 promotional matter), but neither publication nor the current holder of the stamped print is verified. Next action: ask SGPHS/Beaumont Library District which collection holds the stamped print and whether it appeared in company promotional literature (RIGHTS-RULES rule 10).

img_f525afa6dc4390a8.description: A very small (170×214 px) thumbnail of the front page of The Gateway Gazette of Beaumont for Thursday, April 30, 1908. The Gateway Gazette was Beaumont's boom-era weekly: the Riverside Enterprise of Jan. 22, 1908 announced 'the first number of the Gateway Gazette, a new weekly paper, will be issued at Beaumont' the next day, naming Arthur J. Burdick of the Gateway Gazette in its Personals, and the Los Angeles Herald of Jan. 26, 1908 confirmed the new paper 'made its appearance last Thursday' (Jan. 23, 1908). Number 15 on April 30 is exactly 14 weeks after that first issue, corroborating the date. The issue also reports an S.P. general manager's special-train visit and the Beaumont women's Orange Festival.

img_7cc7f95ae75d9aa6.title: Southern Pacific depot, Beaumont, California — real-photo postcard, postmarked March 28, 1909
img_7cc7f95ae75d9aa6.description: Tinted real-photo postcard of the Southern Pacific depot at Beaumont, California, with thirteen men and boys — at least five holding bicycles — posed on the platform, a steaming train at right, and San Gorgonio Pass foothills in the distance. The station board reads 'To San Francisco 562 7/10 M. / B[ea]umont / [Elev]ation 2556 Feet / To New Orleans 1925 4/10 M.' (the SP Sunset Route mileage format), and 'S.P. Depot Beaumont' is written along the bottom. The card was mailed to Miss Lula Wheeler of Melrose, Texas ('How are you I am fine Come where oranges grow, Hudson Hall') and is dated by its March 28, 1909 postmark; the arc cancel visible on the catalog copy reads '…GDOCHES' — Nacogdoches, the town nearest Melrose — matching that transit. Because it is a 'Beaumont' card it entered the Tyrrell Historical Library in Beaumont, TEXAS (Southeast Texas Postcards Collection), whose own catalog record confirms the subject is Beaumont, California, noting the two Beaumonts 'are sometimes mistaken for one another'; the mountainous backdrop is impossible for coastal-plain Beaumont, Texas. The catalog's copy is a 729×461 screenshot watermarked 'TYRRELL HISTORICAL LIBRARY'; The Portal to Texas History serves an unwatermarked 1500×980 scan of the front (and 1500×990 of the back). The previous credit 'Tyrrell Historical Library / Calisphere' was wrong about Calisphere — the digitization is a Portal to Texas History item.

img_e5061c07708726ac.title: 'Spectacular Fire at Beaumont Destroys Hotel Edinburgh' — Los Angeles Herald, August 18, 1909
img_e5061c07708726ac.description: Page 6 of the Los Angeles Herald of Wednesday, August 18, 1909, dominated by 'Spectacular Fire at Beaumont Destroys Hotel Edinburgh, Landmark of Community' with a halftone of the hotel; the page layout in the catalog image (including 'Would Educate All Foreigners', 'Very Human Is Royal Family' and the Globe Savings Bank advertisement) matches the CDNC scan. The article (dateline Beaumont, Aug. 17) reports the three-story, 70-room frame hotel — 'the next largest hotel building in Riverside county' — totally destroyed about 11 o'clock the previous night, i.e. the night of August 16–17, 1909, a $45,000–$50,000 loss against $10,000 insurance; operator David Cochrane (formerly of Riverside's Hotel Hollyrood) was away, though his wife was in the building, and the four-acre park's trees were scorched. The Herald recounts that F. P. Sigler, 'original founder of the town of Beaumont,' spent $44,000 on the hotel (the Herald says built 1890; a Feb. 1908 Gazette retrospective shows the same house advertised as the 'Beaumont' hotel in a Sentinel of about 1888 and 'now known as Hotel Edinburgh'), lost it in the 1893 panic to a San Francisco bank, after which it stood closed until the Beaumont Land and Water Company bought hotel, townsite, lands and water in August 1907 and refurnished it. The record therefore depicts a newspaper page, not an original photograph: its date is the publication date, and the hotel's name at destruction was Hotel Edinburgh — 'Beaumont Hotel' was the building's original 1880s name.

img_02861b7cd39cd162.title: Fifth Street at Egan Avenue with A. T. Gantt's general merchandise store, Beaumont, c. 1910
img_02861b7cd39cd162.description: A modern smartphone capture (4032×3024; the holder's thumb is visible) of an original print mounted on the black paper of an unidentified album, showing a crowd in a wide dirt intersection — per the filename, Fifth Street looking east at Egan Avenue, Beaumont. A four-horse coach loaded with men and boys stands at left before spectators, several women wearing the wide-brimmed hats of c. 1910; buggies and a wagon wait at right in front of a two-story false-front store whose corner signs read 'A.T. G…' and 'GENERAL M[ERCHANDISE]'. That is A. T. Gantt & Bro., 'Get It at Gantt's', which advertised general merchandise from the Gateway Gazette's first issue (Jan. 23, 1908) onward; the Gantt building stood on Egan Avenue just south of Fifth Street (423 Egan) until it was wrecked in March 1940, which supports the filename's placement of the camera at Fifth and Egan. Across the street a large billboard and a porch sign each end 'BEAUMONT, CAL.', and an August 1908 Gazette photo-feature describes this same business block as 'showing the postoffice and one of two large general merchandise stores.' The occasion — plausibly a parade or one of the land company's excursion parties of the boom years — is not identified.
img_02861b7cd39cd162.rights: Unpublished snapshot by an unknown photographer, c. 1910, in an unidentified private album. As an anonymous unpublished work its U.S. copyright runs 120 years from creation (expiring c. 2030 if taken in 1910), and the album's owner is unidentified, so neither PD status nor a permission contact can yet be named. img_50e61a8496f4bfd2.title: WCTU Fountain dedication, Fifth Street and Egan Avenue, Beaumont — December 25, 1910
img_50e61a8496f4bfd2.description: Real-photo postcard, hand-titled on the negative "W.C.T.U. Fountain Beaumont Calif", showing roughly two dozen women in dark Edwardian dress and wide-brimmed hats — with a few children and a dog — gathered at a four-columned, tile-roofed pavilion sheltering a fieldstone drinking fountain, a clapboard building behind. The Woman's Christian Temperance Union presented the fountain to Beaumont at Fifth Street and Egan Avenue and dedicated it on Christmas Day, December 25, 1910 — a date confirmed independently by a 1959 Record Gazette retrospective, a 2011 Press-Enterprise centennial piece, and the City of Beaumont's own account of the plaque reading "WCTU Dec. 25, 1910". The Rios-collection provenance identifies this as the dedication gathering itself. The fountain survives: it now stands in the triangular Veterans (Triangle) Park at Egan Avenue and Seventh Street, and modern photographs of it appear elsewhere in this collection. The catalog's 6,926-px scan is byte-identical to the Beaumont Library District copy whose filename credits the Leslie A. Rios III postcard collection.

img_0b3ce9bbcc89c40d.title: Fifth Street at Egan Avenue with the Bank of Beaumont — Frasher Foto postcard, c. late 1920s
img_0b3ce9bbcc89c40d.description: Real-photo postcard imprinted "STREET SCENE — BEAUMONT, CALIF / FRASHERS FOTO — POMONA", a product of Burton Frasher Sr.'s prolific Pomona postcard operation whose negative collection is held by the Pomona Public Library. The view runs along Fifth Street: at right stands the classical arched-portal Bank of Beaumont building — the same structure shown in a Banning Library District print labeled "Bank of Beaumont Fifth St. and Egan Ave." — while the left sidewalk shows a jeweler's bracket clock, a barber pole, a drugstore sign, a projecting CAFE sign, and an American flag, with strings of pennants and flags (one bearing a sun disc) crossing the street for some celebration. A later hand added "Main Street, Beaumont, California. Circa 1925" in the lower margin; Frasher's own caption says only "Street Scene". img_c323e4a9718d30b7.title: Emeteria and Luis Estrada, Beaumont — 1940s
img_c323e4a9718d30b7.description: Formal portrait of Emeteria and Luis Estrada standing before a hung cloth backdrop on a patterned carpet — she in a polka-dot short-sleeved dress, he in a suit with a lapel pin, his arm around her shoulder — dated to the 1940s by the Estrada family provenance carried in the collection filename. Luis Estrada was a longtime Southern Pacific Railroad section worker in Beaumont; companion photographs in the same BLD folder show him among rail crews ("Railroad workers Luis Estrada fourth from right", "Railworkers Luis Estrada far right") and the family at dinner inside their SP section house. The couple was photographed together again decades later ("Emeteria and Luis Estrada 1970s.jpg"). Beaumont later named Luis Estrada Road, off Veile Avenue near the tracks, in his honor — a collection photo shows some sixty family members gathered under the street sign celebrating the naming's 20th anniversary in 2021, dating the naming to about 2001 — and family photos also document a life-size track-worker figure at the California State Railroad Museum in Sacramento that the family identifies with him. The catalog scan is byte-identical to the BLD folder original.

img_0880ba793548d705.title: Fifth Street (Main Street), Beaumont, with Harvey's Cafe and the Beaumont Garage — real photo postcard, c. 1932-1940
img_0880ba793548d705.original_title: Steve Lech Postcard Of Fifth Street
img_0880ba793548d705.description: Real photo postcard captioned "Fifth Street (Main) Beaumont, Calif." in the negative, looking along Beaumont's principal business street. At left are a painted wall advertisement for The Gazette ("The home paper for [number obscured] years / advertising [and] commercial printing"), the sign of Harvey's Cafe, and parked sedans of c. 1929-1931 vintage; at right are another cafe, a barber shop, and the Beaumont Garage ("Welding and Machine Work") with a vertical Gilmore Gasoline sign. Harvey's Cafe, run by Harvey O'Day on West Fifth Street between Egan and Wellwood avenues and later Beaumont's bus depot, first appears in the Daily Gazette on 6 October 1932 and is absent from the digitized 1928-1931 issues, so the view is c. 1932 at the earliest; the cafe's old building was remodeled for other use in 1944. The Beaumont Garage was a much older institution, advertising "Now Open for Business" (W. D. Lewis, manager) in October 1908, trading as Beaumont Garage & Machine Works by 1916, and purchased by M. Woodland in 1928. The scan carries the "RivCoKid Images" watermark of Riverside County historian Steve Lech, whose postcard collection supplied it. The catalog's previous 1908-1925 dating is impossible given the automobiles and Harvey's Cafe signage.

img_4239365a9df07707.title: 5th Street at the A. T. Gantt & Bro. corner, Beaumont — real photo postcard, c. 1915-1925
img_4239365a9df07707.description: Real photo postcard (rubber-stamped "5th street / BEAUMONT" in red, captioned "Beaumont. Cal." in the negative) showing touring cars of the mid-1910s to early 1920s parked along a business corner, with children on the sidewalk at right. The porch sign at right reads "A. T. GANTT AND BRO. / GROCERIES - DRY GOODS": A. T. Gantt & Bro. general merchandise advertised in the Beaumont Gazette from January 1908, and the Gantt mercantile at Fifth Street and Egan Avenue was established after the family's 1906 arrival, continuing under Mrs. Brice Gantt after her husband's death c. 1927 (her 1936 obituary). Across the street, a rusticated cement-block business row carries two REAL ESTATE signs and a round sweet-shop/cigar sign — cement-block commercial construction that Beaumont adopted in 1907-08. This is the Beaumont Library District's Calisphere item CBEA_036, whose description names "Gantt, a groceries and dry goods store, a Sweet Shop offering lunches and a real estate store front" and places the view (with BLD's own question mark) on the 200 block of West 5th Street between Grace and Egan — the district around Fifth & Egan near the depot that was early Beaumont's main business section.

img_03ae9abaca02013c.title: Interior of the S. and S. Grocery, Egan Avenue and Fifth Street, Beaumont, c. 1930
img_03ae9abaca02013c.original_title: George Sumner S And S Store On Fifth Street Interior
img_03ae9abaca02013c.description: Interior of a well-stocked 1920s-era grocery, identified by the collection title as George Sumner's S. and S. store: a produce island stands mid-floor, canned goods line the right wall, and four people pose — two men in shirtsleeves and vests at center, and a mustached man with a bobbed-haired woman behind the counter at right. Wall advertising includes a Kellogg's Krumbles sign ("Build the body with nature's food"), a Kellogg's Bran poster, Alpine Milk tin signs, a Pearl Oil (kerosene) can, a coffee poster ("It's the best I ever tasted"), and National Biscuit Company cartons bearing the "Uneeda Bakers" slogan the company adopted in 1923. The Daily Gazette documents the S. and S. Grocery at the "Corner Egan and Fifth Sts." in weekly ads through 1928, run by George R. Sumner ("Mr. Sumner of the S. & S. Grocery," 22 Mar 1928) with his son-in-law as partner; by January 1931 it advertised as Orange Empire Store No. 25, and by February 1935 the W. M. McDaris family ran it. A November 1928 note about "the grocery now known as the S. & S. grocery" indicates the name — plausibly Sumner & son-in-law — was then fairly new. The store is not among the Beaumont Library District's Calisphere items (searched 2026-07-21).

img_88e0efbd8026acce.title: South side of West 5th Street, Beaumont — Crowther Real Estate, Beaumont Variety Store, Pass City Grocery, and Maloof's, c. 1933-1937
img_88e0efbd8026acce.description: A brick commercial row on the south side of the 200 block of West 5th Street between Grace and Egan (per the Beaumont Library District's own catalog record), with an early-1930s coupe at the curb. Signs read, right to left: BARBER SHOP; CHARLES E. CROWTHER REAL ESTATE (with insurance lettering on the window) — Crowther appears in Beaumont press from 1915 and was a fixture of its 1930s real estate trade; a GRUNOW appliance window sign (a brand marketed c. 1933-1937); the BEAUMONT VARIETY STOR[E] awning (O. R. Chadsey's "Sells for Less" dry goods store, in press 1928-1954); PASS CITY GROCERY (Orange Empire Store No. 208, Peck & Peck, props.); and the oval hanging sign of MALOOF'S men's and women's shop. The Maloof Department Store (J. P. Maloof & Bro. of Banning) opened in Beaumont's Smoot building near the post office in mid-May 1933, so the photograph cannot predate that — correcting the catalog's 1929-1933 range. This is Calisphere BLD item CBEA_101, whose description names the same businesses.

img_4ec3e978a2772b6b.title: Track Crew on a Railroad Bridge, Luis Estrada Fourth from Right
img_4ec3e978a2772b6b.original_title: Railroad Workers Luis Estrada Fourth From Right
img_4ec3e978a2772b6b.description: Nine trackmen in work shirts, dungarees, and broad-brimmed hats pose in bright sun on a railroad deck bridge with pipe handrails; several lean on long-handled track tools, and a frame gantry (resembling a telltale or crossing structure) stands over the track behind them. The donor filename identifies Luis Estrada as fourth from right. The 1950 U.S. Census records Estrada (age 55, born Mexico, not naturalized) heading a household in Beaumont with wife Emeteria and six California-born children, anchoring his birth to c. 1895 — so the catalog's old 1910–1935 range would show him at 40 or younger, while the man here and the crew's workwear read as late 1930s–1940s. The mixed Anglo and Mexican-American crew is consistent with the section gangs that maintained the Southern Pacific main line through the San Gorgonio Pass, the railroad the Estrada family's own materials associate with Luis. The exact bridge location is unidentified. The 5954x4085 px scan also sits as a duplicate in the client's 'Mexican and other railroad workers' folder.

img_5216d93c22702ca5.description: Color snapshot of the elderly couple standing on a lawn before a house numbered 218: Emeteria in a patterned shirtdress and white shoes, Luis — white-haired and mustached — in a dark suit and tie, both dressed for a formal occasion. The screen door behind them carries a circular ornament that appears to be a letter initial, but whether 218 was the Estradas' own home is unconfirmed. The 1950 census gives their birth years as c. 1895 (Luis) and c. 1908 (Emeteria), both born in Mexico, making them roughly 75–84 and 62–71 here — consistent with the couple shown. Luis, remembered as a longtime Beaumont railroad trackworker, was later honored with a street name: Luis Estrada Road runs through west Beaumont near the rail corridor, and this collection documents the family's 2021 gathering for the naming's 20th anniversary. The catalog's exact '1970' date was an artifact of the filename's '1970s' and has been corrected to the decade.

img_228a900cb9c1637b.description: Real photo postcard by Frasher Fotos of Pomona (the Frasher's logo and negative number F6331 are printed in the margin), captioned 'Beaumont, Calif. on U.S. Highways 60 and 99.' A Greyhound coach loads at the curb outside The Corner Store ('Fountain — Sundries,' with a Greyhound sign on its facade indicating it served as the local bus stop); beyond it stand Eastwood's Market ('Fresh Produce — Meats — Groceries'), an ice-cream-and-sodas shop, the Beaumont Theatre, a feed-and-seed store, and a service station, with late-1930s/early-1940s automobiles in lanes stenciled 'SCHOOL.' The theatre marquee advertises Dorothy Lamour in 'Masquerade in Mexico' — a Paramount picture released December 3, 1945 — on a double bill with the 1940 Warner Bros. title 'City for Conquest,' which dates the exposure to c. 1946. Sixth Street carried the combined US 60/99 highway traffic through Beaumont, which is why Frasher's roadside series covered this strip. Scanned from a card in the Leslie A. Rios III postcard collection.

The cafe's address put it on the U.S. 60-70-99 highway strip at the east end of Beaumont, among the motels, cafes, and gas stations this folder documents. Nothing further about Joe's Cafe or its proprietor could be confirmed online this session; city directories and Record-Gazette advertising are the concrete next step. The filename's 'strike side' refers to the matchbook's striker, not to a labor action.

img_5a70b41831a92160.title: Sixth Street (then U.S. Highway 99), from the 1946 Beaumont High School annual
img_5a70b41831a92160.original_title: 6Th St Fr Bmt High Yearbook Donated By Leslie Rios
img_5a70b41831a92160.description: A photographed page from the 1946 Beaumont High School annual: a halftone street view printed above the start of the yearbook's index (the heading 'Index' and the first senior entries, beginning 'Smith, Pat,' are visible below the image). The photograph looks across a wide intersection on Sixth Street, Beaumont's main commercial street, which carried U.S. Highway 99 through town before the freeway era — Wikipedia's San Gorgonio Pass article documents 6th Street in Beaumont as an old section of U.S. 99. On the left corner is a Standard Stations, Inc. service station beneath a Chevron 'Supreme Gasoline' billboard; beyond it a storefront signed '—ING CENTER' carries a Coca-Cola sign, and at the right edge a Mobilgas shield with the Flying Red Horse marks a competing station — a gasoline strip typical of a US 99 highway town. Every legible automobile is a prewar model, consistent with an exposure around 1945–46, when the annual went to press before postwar cars were common on the street. The catalog copy is a handheld phone photo (4032×3024) of the printed page from the yearbook Leslie A. Rios III donated in November 2020, not a scan of an original print.

img_c228028c8fdfc647.title: Beaumont Union High School band with school banner, from the 1949 annual
img_c228028c8fdfc647.original_title: Band Fr Bmt High Yearbook Donated By Leslie Rios
img_c228028c8fdfc647.description: Roughly sixty uniformed musicians of the Beaumont Union High School band pose in rows on the steps of a two-story school building beneath a hanging banner lettered 'BEAUMONT UNION HIGH SCHOOL BAND' (legible under magnification of the master file), with sousaphones at the rear corners, majorette-uniformed girls kneeling at the flanks, and a drum majorette and a small mascot girl seated front and center among the bass drums. 'Beaumont Union High School' was the school's formal name in this era — a Record-Gazette obituary records a 1943 graduate under that name. The page comes from the 1949 annual, so the photograph dates to the 1948–49 school year. The building behind the band is presumably on the historic BHS campus — Beaumont's first high school building went up in 1911, and the Record-Gazette described BHS's '107-year-old campus' still hosting football in 2018 — but the source folder's claim that the old high school is 'now City Hall' has not been independently verified; the Beaumont Civic Center campus is documented to incorporate former school-district property (the old Summit School parcel behind the Civic Center, bought by the city in 2009). The catalog copy is a phone photo of the printed yearbook page from the volume donated by Leslie A. Rios III in November 2020.

img_6b0ff0ed19b0fb9e.title: Ramona V. Torres — c. 1940s portrait as reproduced on the Ramona's Restaurant menu
img_6b0ff0ed19b0fb9e.description: Rephotographed detail of a laminated Ramona's Restaurant menu bearing the black-and-white portrait of a young Ramona V. Torres (née Velasquez, 1917-2005), flowers pinned in her curled 1940s-style hair; the partial red side-panel text ('For three… passed…') is the menu's family-history blurb. Ramona was born Jan. 24, 1917 in Douglas, Arizona, married Frank Mora Torres in Los Angeles on Feb. 24, 1935, and in 1972 the couple opened Ramona's Restaurant at 249 W. Sixth St., Beaumont. Press coverage of the restaurant's Jan. 11, 2025 closing noted that her black-and-white portrait 'hangs on a wall in the dining room and decorates the menu' — this image is that menu reproduction. The restaurant ran 52 years under three generations: the founders, then daughter Christine and Gil Vargas Sr. from about 1982, then grandchildren Gil Jr., Adrian and Maritza Vargas until closing. The underlying portrait likely dates from about the 1940s, when Ramona was in her twenties; the physical menu photographed here is modern, from the restaurant's final years.

In 1972 they opened Ramona's Restaurant at 249 W. Sixth St., Beaumont, which their daughter Christine's family — the Vargases — carried through three generations until it closed Jan. 11, 2025 after 52 years. Their apparent ages here (Frank looks roughly 55-65) and Ramona's tall bouffant suggest the photo was taken around 1970, near the era they founded the restaurant. The occasion is unrecorded.

img_4e6f8597cedbda5b.title: Jane Eyer Smoot (1859-1935) — printed book plate captioned "Mrs. Kenneth R. Smoot"
img_4e6f8597cedbda5b.description: Scan of a printed book page: a halftone portrait plate captioned "MRS. KENNETH R. SMOOT" showing Jane Eyer Smoot (Dec. 17, 1859 - Nov. 25, 1935) white-haired, in a wide-collared dress of the mid-1910s-early 1920s, with the book's binding edge visible at right. Born in Dwight, Illinois, to Daniel Eyer, a Salt Lake City mining man, and Nancy Bennett Eyer, she graduated from the University of Michigan in 1881, married attorney Kenneth R. Smoot in 1883, and in 1894 became president of Highland Park, Illinois' first known woman's club (the Monday Club, renamed the Ossoli Club that October), advocating for woman suffrage in the 1890s. In Beaumont — where her brother Clarendon B. Eyer was president and her husband vice president of the Beaumont Land and Water Company, and where Kenneth later headed the Bank of Beaumont — she remained a civic force: the Beaumont Daily Gazette of May 26, 1932 ran "Tribute Paid to Mrs. K. R. Smoot for Leadership," crediting her and Miss Boulton with the petition crusade that brought gas service to the San Gorgonio Pass. The volume this plate comes from has not been identified; her apparent age and the plate's typography suggest publication c. 1915-1930. She died in Beaumont and is buried at Hillside Memorial Park, Redlands.

Eyer's death at the Smoot home at 603 Esplanade, Redondo Beach; by April 1909 her husband Kenneth was vice president and her brother Clarendon B. Eyer president of the Beaumont Land and Water Company, the firm behind Beaumont's land boom. McLaughlin in 2019. Jane died in Beaumont on November 25, 1935, three years after Kenneth, and is buried beside him at Hillside Memorial Park, Redlands.

img_317c261e7e95cb9d.title: Kenneth R. Smoot and Jane Eyer Smoot — joint photo from Kenneth's 1920 U.S. passport application
img_317c261e7e95cb9d.original_title: Kenneth Russell Smoot And Jane Eyer Smoot
img_317c261e7e95cb9d.description: Joint photograph of Kenneth Russell Smoot (Apr. 18, 1857 - May 29, 1932) and Jane Eyer Smoot (1859-1935) with Kenneth's cursive signature above, pixel-identical to the 295x295 px Find a Grave image captioned "Kenneth R Smoot and wife Jane Eyer Smoot Passport photo." It comes from Kenneth's U.S. passport application — his passport was issued November 29, 1920, residence Beaumont, California — in the era when a wife traveling with her husband was commonly included on his passport, so couples were photographed together on one application. Kenneth, born in Washington, D.C. to Dr. Samuel Clement Smoot, attended the University of Michigan, practiced law, and compiled the 'Revised Ordinances of the City of Highland Park' (Illinois) before moving west: by April 1909 he was vice president of the Beaumont Land and Water Company — whose sole stockholders were himself, his brother-in-law Clarendon B. Eyer (president), and John D. Reavis — the family firm behind Beaumont's land boom, with subsidiary San Gorgonio Water Company. He served as president of the Bank of Beaumont until resigning for ill health on March 18, 1932, succeeded by R. P. Stewart, and his Beaumont Daily Gazette obituary called him "one of the city's builders"; he died that May 29 at his home "Quenjuana" on la Mesa Miravilla and is buried at Hillside Memorial Park, Redlands. The couple's son Clement Eyer Smoot (1884-1963), later founder of the Smoot-Holman Company, won team golf gold at the 1904 Olympics.

img_291537b3068812cf.title: Clarendon B. Eyer, president of the Beaumont Land and Water Company
img_291537b3068812cf.description: Signed passport-style portrait of Clarendon B. Eyer, the capitalist who as president of the Beaumont Land and Water Company led the syndicate that bought the Beaumont townsite and adjoining lands from a San Francisco bank on August 2, 1907 and relaunched the town. The company's directors and sole stockholders were Eyer and his brothers-in-law Kenneth R. Smoot (vice president) and John D. Reavis — a family enterprise built on the fortune of Eyer's father Daniel Eyer, 'a wealthy mining man of Salt Lake City' (Los Angeles Herald obituary of Eyer's mother, Dec. 7, 1908); Eyer himself was dealing in Salt Lake City real estate in 1906 and told a December 1907 banquet he had come to California from Chicago. From offices at 616 South Broadway, Los Angeles, he ran the land sales, water development, and a forty-newspaper advertising campaign of Beaumont's 1907-1915 apple-boom era, and in April 1908 began a residence for himself at Sixth Street and Magnolia Avenue in Beaumont. The print bears Eyer's signature across the top and an embossed seal at right — the format of a U.S. passport application photograph (photos required from December 1914) — and he appears markedly older here than in his published April 11, 1909 Los Angeles Herald portrait, suggesting c. 1915-1925. His birth and death dates remain unverified.

img_dbf7e0bb619c1c74.title: Cora K. Eyer (Mrs. Clarendon B. Eyer)
img_dbf7e0bb619c1c74.description: Signed passport-style portrait of Cora K. Eyer, almost certainly Mrs. C. B. Eyer, wife of Beaumont Land and Water Company president Clarendon B. Eyer — the 1908 obituary of Clarendon's mother names his daughters as Marguerite and Eleanor, leaving the wife as the household's adult 'Mrs. C. B. Eyer.' She was an active builder in boom-era Beaumont in her own right: by February 1909 she had taken permits for four cottages in the townsite (Los Angeles Herald, Dec. 13, 1908 and Feb. 28, 1909), and in May 1910 she and daughter Marguerite sailed for Asia aboard the S.S. Mongolia. The name inscribed across the top matches U.S. passport-application photo conventions (photos required from December 1914), the same format as the companion Clarendon B. Eyer portrait in this folder, giving an estimated date of c. 1915-1925. Her 'K.' may be a maiden-name initial — the Eyers' son was named Knowlton K. Eyer — but her maiden name and vital dates remain unverified.

img_2fa19df607bf43e1.description: Letterpress halftone, printed in blue ink beneath the headline 'HOME OF C. B. EYER,' showing the broad-gabled, single-story residence of Beaumont Land and Water Company president Clarendon B. Eyer behind young garden plantings. In April 1908 the Los Angeles Herald reported that Eyer 'has selected 104x120 feet at Sixth street and Magnolia avenue as the site for a residence, the plans for which are being prepared,' so this is very probably that house, photographed after construction c. 1908-09. The halftone screen, ruled border, and display-type headline mark the scan as a clipping from a printed publication — most likely one of the company's promotional pieces or a pictorial page from its 1908-1915 campaign, which the Herald said ran in 'nearly forty newspapers.' The catalog's previous 'circa 1915-1920' date derived only from the scan's filename; the documented 1908 construction start and the promotional-era publication context support c. 1908-1915 instead. The specific publication this clipping came from has not yet been identified.

img_1d5ad1237f7755e2.title: Our Lady of Guadalupe Chapel (later Sacred Heart), Beaumont barrio, c. 1930-1955
img_1d5ad1237f7755e2.original_title: Barrio Church Sacred Heart Parish Fr Grace Granados
img_1d5ad1237f7755e2.description: A small whitewashed chapel with a squat arched bell gable topped by a cross stands beside a dirt street in Beaumont's Mexican-American barrio, a plain hip-roofed house behind it and a bare winter tree overhead. This is consistent with the original barrio chapel at Olive and B Street, south of Highway 60 and west of Beaumont Avenue, which opened in 1930 as Our Lady of Guadalupe Chapel to serve the Hispanic community of Beaumont and Banning, many of whom worked on the nearby railroad (Diocese of San Bernardino archivist Peter Bradley). For over 25 years it operated as a mission of San Gorgonio Parish in Beaumont and Precious Blood Parish in Banning, until a second church was built on the site in 1956 and the mission was erected as Sacred Heart Parish. The 'Fr' in the working title is donor shorthand for 'from' — the print came from Grace Granados in June 2025 — not a priest's name. The primitive setting and print quality suggest the chapel-era decades before the 1956 replacement.

img_22f62627c5d79f7e.title: Sacred Heart Church (built 1956), Beaumont barrio — printed halftone reproduction
img_22f62627c5d79f7e.original_title: Sared Heart Parish In Beaumont Barrio Date
img_22f62627c5d79f7e.description: A printed halftone reproduction (visible CMYK registration fringing indicates a scan from a publication, not an original print) showing the second Sacred Heart church: a gable-fronted stucco building with a round window over the entrance, a corner bell tower with open belfry, pyramidal tile cap and cross, and a small tile-roofed outbuilding at right. The massing, round window, corner tower, and outbuilding match the church in the Leslie A. Rios III color slide of this parish, identifying it as the second church built in 1956 at Olive and B Street, when the 25-year-old Our Lady of Guadalupe mission was erected as Sacred Heart Parish. Rev. Felix Callymore was its first pastor (1956-1962), followed by Rev. Andre Begeron (1962, 1963-1964); the parish was poor — Sunday collections totaled about $8 — and after San Gorgonio Parish completed its own new church in 1958, membership drained away. The Diocese of San Diego closed Sacred Heart Parish on March 5, 1964, and the building was sold to a local Catholic family for $4,000. The photograph therefore most likely dates from the parish's 1956-1964 lifetime, reproduced later in an unidentified newspaper or newsletter.

img_add874f3a7967842.title: Congregation leaving Sacred Heart Church, Beaumont barrio, c. 1956-1962
img_add874f3a7967842.original_title: Sacred Heart Barrio Church From Leslie Rios
img_add874f3a7967842.description: A color slide-era view of families in Sunday best leaving Sacred Heart Church in Beaumont's barrio: girls in white First Communion-style dresses with veils and floral headpieces, a girl in a blue coat, boys in white shirts, and women in 1950s coats and headscarves on wet pavement. The church is the second building, constructed in 1956 at Olive and B Street when the Our Lady of Guadalupe mission was erected as Sacred Heart Parish — textured white stucco, red mission-tile trim, round stained-glass window over the canopied door, and a corner tower with a Virgin statue in its niche. A light-blue mid-1950s Chevrolet at left carries a 1956-issue yellow California plate (CWE 630), the base used through 1962 before the 1963 gold-on-black plates, and a dark early-1950s Chrysler-family sedan sits at right, bracketing the photo between the 1956 construction and 1962. The parish, whose members largely worked on the railroad, was closed by the Diocese of San Diego on March 5, 1964, making this one of the few color records of its short life as a full parish.

The settlement is a thin scatter of frame buildings on a treeless plain, and the large multi-story block at its right (east) edge is identified by the collection as the Hotel Beaumont — the 'beautiful and costly' hotel the Southern California Investment Co. built in 1887 as the town's third hotel to attract land buyers, which 'stood unused for years' after the 1888 boom collapse and was destroyed by a kitchen fire in 1909. The standing hotel brackets the view between 1887 and 1909, and the town's sparseness suggests the earlier half of that range. A handwritten negative number reading '2099' shows at lower left — the mark of a commercial view photographer's numbered series (the C.C. Pierce / California Historical Society series at USC uses corner numbers of this kind), not yet identified. The 960 × 733 px digital file is consistent with a web download from an online library rather than an in-house scan.

Across the open dirt forecourt, where a horse team stands, is Peter Allen's false-fronted general store, its parapet signed 'STORE' and its porch fascia 'PETER ALLEN' over goods and figures under the awning; a second scallop-parapeted false-front store stands to its right (sign not legible at this resolution), with a windmill and the scattered cottages of the young town on the treeless plain behind. On the knoll at far right rises the three-story, tower-and-cupola-topped Hotel Beaumont, built 1887 by the Southern California Investment Co. and destroyed by a kitchen fire in 1909, which brackets the scene between 1887 and August 1909. The scan came from the Karen Sumner Noordman collection in January 2023; only the card front is present in the archive.

img_e223c8fe27b85e0d.title: Reznor Perry Stewart, studio portrait
img_e223c8fe27b85e0d.description: Vignetted studio bust portrait of Reznor Perry Stewart in a striped sack suit and patterned four-in-hand tie, with a full greying beard and swept-back hair. Stewart homesteaded at Beaumont in 1883 and, adding purchased Southern Pacific railroad land, built a grain and hay ranch of about 2,200 acres — one of the pass's major operations; Holmes' 1912 county history records that 'R. P. Stewart and Dan Scott commenced raising grain' in 1884, the year settlement began in earnest. He went on to be a founder and long-time president of the Beaumont Bank (built 1911 in the Funk Building, 248 W. 5th St.), and the family name survives in Stewart Park (named in his honor, per SGPHS) and on the 'Stewart Sunny Slope Cemetery' entrance arch; his daughter Laura May Stewart appears with him in SGPHS ranch photographs, and Stewart-family material at the Beaumont Library District carries Laura May Stewart Trust rights. The vignetted cabinet-style format and his costume suggest the 1890s-1900s; his birth and death dates were not located in the sources searched this session.

img_06355ab9cdf953fb.description: Newsprint clipping from page 3 of The Daily Record-Gazette of Tuesday, April 30, 1968, carrying a staff photograph (credited 'Record-Gazette Photo') of the Stewart Sunnyslope Cemetery entrance: a wrought-iron arch lettered 'STEWART SUNNY SLOPE CEMETERY' springs between two rough-stone pylons joined by low stone walls and chain-link fencing, with mature shade trees and the cemetery's cypresses beyond. The cemetery's name ties to Beaumont's pioneer Stewart family — Reznor Perry Stewart homesteaded in 1883 and the collection files this clipping in its Stewart folder — though the documentation of the naming itself remains to be pulled.

img_f711da54b73a8423.description: Blue-monochrome halftone postcard captioned "The office of the Gateway Gazette as it now appears, Beaumont, Cal.", showing the paper's small false-front frame office with plate-glass show windows, a recessed entry, and a partly obscured roofline sign reading "[Gatew]ay Gazette". The Gateway Gazette was Beaumont's weekly newspaper, launched during the town's 1907-09 land boom: the Los Angeles Herald of January 19, 1908 reported that "the building for the new printing establishment is about completed and next Thursday the first issue of the Gateway Gazette, a Beaumont paper, will be added to the state's newspaper list, under the editorship of Arthur J. Burdick, formerly one of the editors of the Los Angeles Evening News." A full-page Beaumont Land and Water Company promotion in the Herald of April 13, 1908 quotes "the Gateway Gazette, Beaumont's weekly newspaper" on the town's bank organization, gas-and-electric company, and new volunteer fire department, and Burdick was still bylined "Editor Beaumont Gateway Gazette" in the Herald of July 18, 1909. The "as it now appears" phrasing and the boom-era promotional style date the card to the paper's early years, when the purpose-built office (completed January 1908) was new. A companion card in the same collection shows the composing room interior (img_19665af80792888c).

img_19665af80792888c.title: Gateway Gazette composing room, Beaumont (booster postcard with typesetter's note)
img_19665af80792888c.original_title: Gateway Gazette Interior Postcard Leslie Rios
img_19665af80792888c.description: Blue-monochrome halftone postcard captioned "A corner in the Gateway Gazette composing room, Beaumont, Cal.", showing the interior of the weekly paper's plant: banks of type cases along the left wall, sloped composing benches with more cases at right, work tables, and a man — evidently a compositor — standing at left holding a sheet of paper. The Gateway Gazette launched in late January 1908 under editor Arthur J. Burdick in a purpose-built office (LA Herald, Jan 19, 1908) and was still publishing under Burdick in July 1909. A later hand, in blue ink across the right margin, adds a first-person provenance note: "I worked in this place setting type in 1911. My name was Edvige Hamel, now Mrs. Edvige Smith" — direct testimony that the paper's composing room was operating with hand-set type in 1911. The annotation's phrasing ("my name was... now Mrs. ...") and modern ink show it was written years after the card was printed. Companion to the exterior office view img_f711da54b73a8423 in the same collection.

img_8ecf8879b0fffd2d.title: Deodar cedars lining Beaumont Avenue (real photo postcard)

img_8ecf8879b0fffd2d.description: Black-and-white real photo postcard, hand-lettered "BEAUMONT AVE." (lower left) and "BEAUMONT, CALIF" (lower right), looking down the two-lane avenue through its double row of deodar cedars, with a lone postwar sedan receding toward distant hills. The deodars that line both sides of Beaumont Avenue from present Oak Valley Parkway north through Cherry Valley toward Oak Glen were planted in the 1930s and grew into the Pass Area's celebrated "evergreen tunnel," a local landmark residents have repeatedly organized to protect (Record-Gazette). In this frame the trees already stand several times the height of the car — well-established plantings of roughly 15-25 years — which, with the late-1940s body style of the automobile, places the photograph around 1950. The scan was saved from an eBay listing; the card's photographer/publisher and back are unrecorded.

img_676c1d159bb01165.title: City of Beaumont street map showing the Egan-era diagonal streets, c. 1950s
img_676c1d159bb01165.original_title: Beaumont Map Diagonal Streets To Left Were Mapped By George C Egan
img_676c1d159bb01165.description: Printed street map titled 'City of Beaumont, California,' credited in the plate 'Map furnished courtesy Don Stock—Realtor,' with hand-drawn annotations marking U.S. Highways 70/99 and 60, the 'State Highway' to Banning along Sixth Street, the S.P. Railway, an 'Airport' northwest of town, and the '3 Ring Ranch.' Don Stock appears in the Beaumont Gazette from 1949 and as principal of the Grant and Stock realty firm on Fifth Street from early 1950, and the Three Ring Ranch — George and Connie Ring's thoroughbred farm on Beaumont's western outskirts — first appears in the papers in September 1951, so the map dates to roughly the 1950s, before the 1964 renumbering that replaced US 70/99 with Interstate 10. The working title repeats a local tradition that the diagonal streets at lower left were mapped by George C. Egan: Egan built the first store in the townsite (then called San Gorgonio) in June 1884 on California Avenue, came to own nearly the whole townsite, and sold out in fall 1886 to the Southern California Investment Company, which renamed the town Beaumont in 1887. The diagonal grid runs parallel to the Southern Pacific tracks and includes Egan Avenue (named for the pioneer) and Grace Avenue (named for his daughter), so it does preserve the original 1880s San Gorgonio townsite orientation — though Holmes' 1912 county history credits the investment company, not Egan personally, with laying out some twenty miles of streets.

img_e0a4861e5d654fdb.title: Beaumont Avenue under mature street trees, hand-colored postcard
img_e0a4861e5d654fdb.original_title: Eucalyptus Trees In Beaumont Vintage Postcard Looking North On Beaumont Ave
img_e0a4861e5d654fdb.description: Hand-colored printed postcard captioned on its face 'Beaumont Ave., Beaumont, Cal.,' showing the unpaved avenue running between rows of tall mature street trees, with a Craftsman-style house at right and hills in the distance. The working filename identifies the trees as eucalyptus and the view as looking north; neither can be confirmed from the front of the card alone, but Beaumont's signature street trees — eucalyptus and pepper — were planted along roughly twenty miles of newly laid-out streets by the Southern California Investment Company during the 1887 boom, and Holmes' 1912 county history notes the trees had made excellent growth even while most streets sat unused through the town's long post-1888 slump. The Craftsman-style house and the card's hand-tinted, pre-WWI format fit the assigned c. 1908-1915 window — the years when the Beaumont Land and Water Company's 1907 revival under C. B. Eyer brought new houses to the tree-lined avenues.

img_934590dec97e3d15.title: Southern Pacific depot, Beaumont, with arriving train (printed postcard)
img_934590dec97e3d15.original_title: Beaumont Train Depot After Expansion Remodel
img_934590dec97e3d15.description: Black-and-white printed postcard captioned 'Station, Beaumont, Cal.': a steam locomotive pulls in past the two-story, half-timbered Southern Pacific depot while men wait on the platform, a woman in a white shirtwaist stands by the door, and a baggage cart sits at right. A depot and telegraph office were established here in 1875, when the site — then called Summit — marked the highest point on the SP line through San Gorgonio Pass; the original station was 'a small red building,' and the railroad 'built a large depot about 1887' (Holmes 1912), the structure shown here. No source was found for the working title's claim that this view follows an 'expansion remodel' around 1909; the building is best identified as the c. 1887 depot as it stood in the postcard era, c. 1905-1915. It was aging by then: in January 1914 SP assistant superintendent Sloan remarked that 'the S.P. needed a new depot in Beaumont,' preferring a site at the Apex. The 1939 press still located Beaumont's Egan Avenue business center 'north of the Southern Pacific depot.'

img_4b0acbe1458e33c0.title: Bank of Beaumont under construction, Fifth Street and California Avenue, 1908-09 (photo by Salvage)
img_4b0acbe1458e33c0.original_title: First Bank Of Beaumont Construction From Calisphere
img_4b0acbe1458e33c0.description: Album-mounted photograph labeled in type 'Old Bank Building, Fifth and California' and stamped 'Photo by Salvage,' showing the Bank of Beaumont building topped out but not yet roofed — rusticated cement-block first story, brick second story — with the construction crew posed among brick piles and lumber on the dirt street. The bank organized in 1908 with $25,000 capital and deliberately deferred opening until it had its own building: on August 27, 1908 the directors approved a two-story fire-proof cement-and-brick block at Fifth Street and California Avenue and called for bids; contractor George Mayer won the work, subletting the masonry to T. O. M. Jones; and the bank opened its doors in the finished ~$8,000 building on Monday, April 12, 1909. C. B. Eyer and R. P. Stewart sat on the first board with Kenneth R. Smoot among the stockholders — a 1939 retrospective compressed this to 'Eyer and Smoot built the first Bank of Beaumont building' — and by 1939 the building served as irrigation district headquarters. The photographer, Salvage, advertised in Beaumont's Gateway Gazette in December 1908 and left town in June 1909, which together with the construction stage brackets this view to the fall and winter of 1908-09.

img_35a3c2b0b73a7892.title: Architect's rendering of Summit School, Beaumont (Harry T. MacDonald & Associates), c. 1970-1974
img_35a3c2b0b73a7892.description: Snapshot of a framed presentation watercolor showing a long, low, nearly windowless masonry school with vertical wood-tone accent panels, lawns, young trees, a flagpole and figures, with pass foothills behind; the credit plate reads 'Harry T. MacDonald & Associates, Architecture-Planning' and the partially cropped title block reads '[...]REET SCHOOL / [...]IED SCHOOL DISTRICT.' MacDonald was the architect of record for Beaumont's Summit School: he was introduced at its dedication on May 19, 1974, and the Beaumont Unified School District board accepted the completed school in late February 1974, so this rendering belongs to the design/construction phase, c. 1970-74. Summit School replaced the adjacent Sixth Street School — the 1928 high school building that failed Field Act earthquake standards and was sold to the city to become the Beaumont Civic Center — which is very likely the '...Street School' working title on the cropped label, applied before the board adopted the historic Summit name. That name reaches back to the pioneer Summit School District, organized when the Beaumont area was still in San Bernardino County; the district's 1890 school bell was inscribed 'Bought for Summit School District, San Bernardino County, Cal.' The campus, behind the Civic Center between Orange and Palm avenues, was built on nearly the exact site of the earlier Magnolia School, later housed Mountain View Middle School, and was ultimately sold to the city of Beaumont for its civic-center campus.

img_bad44539e3bf4b42.title: Miss Pritchett's kindergarten class, Wellwood School, Beaumont, 1971-72
img_bad44539e3bf4b42.description: Color class portrait of roughly 33 kindergartners posed in four rows on a lawn beneath autumn-colored trees, their young teacher standing at right, with a black letter-board reading 'WELLWOOD SCHOOL / MISS PRITCHETT / KINDERGARTEN / 1971-72.' The teacher is very probably Penny Pritchett, recorded in the San Bernardino Sun of September 1, 1974 as a teacher at Wellwood School in Beaumont. Wellwood School stood near Seventh Street and Elm Avenue and was one of Beaumont's two long-running elementary campuses alongside Palm School; it descended from the 1890 'Olive school' of the pioneer Summit School District, whose bell was inscribed 'Bought for Summit School District, San Bernardino County, Cal.' By this era it was a Beaumont Unified School District school — Anne Pickett, later BUSD superintendent, taught at Wellwood and served as principal of Wellwood and Palm in the 1970s-80s. The fall foliage indicates the standard autumn sitting, so the photograph was probably taken in October-November 1971 by an as-yet-unidentified school portrait studio.

img_3b097e0808432587.title: Women's railroad track crew ("Female R.R. Crew"), Beaumont
img_3b097e0808432587.original_title: Beaumont Railroad Women Swept The Tracks
img_3b097e0808432587.description: Thirteen women in work shirts, trousers and broad-brimmed hats pose on the railroad right-of-way at Beaumont, at least one holding a track maul; a period ink inscription across the top of the print reads 'Female R.R. Crew', with a first name written above or beside each woman. Legible names in the standing row read Margarita (or Marguerite), Estella, Felicitas, Esther, Emilia, Lupe, Viola(?), and Soledad; the kneeling row includes Lily, Tresie(?), Mary, and Minnie (right margin). The predominantly Spanish given names are consistent with the Mexican-American railroad families of Beaumont's barrio who staffed Southern Pacific's Sunset Route section gangs (compare the catalog's Estrada section-house photographs). Women's track maintenance crews were essentially a WWII labor-shortage phenomenon — roughly 116,000 women worked U.S. railroads by war's end, and Southern Pacific documented hiring Mexican-American women as track workers ('traqueras') — so the photo almost certainly dates c. 1942-1945, not the 1915-1940 range previously carried. The photographer and the family that contributed the print are unrecorded.

img_c8be9dda2808f47c.title: Bogart House in deep snow, Beaumont
img_c8be9dda2808f47c.original_title: Bogart House From Beaumont Library District
img_c8be9dda2808f47c.description: A large two-story clapboard house stands in heavy snow behind bare deciduous trees, with a small porch at its right-hand entrance, a ladder against the near corner, and outbuildings visible at left — identified in the collection as the Bogart House. Guy Bogart (1883-1957) came to California in 1913 and during the 1920s built his Beaumont home and the Cherry Tree Apartments; he served as Beaumont's mayor and councilman, organized the Cherry Blossom Festival at what became Bogart Park in Cherry Valley, and made his home a gathering place for playwrights, socialists and authors including Upton Sinclair. He died in 1957 and is buried at Stewart Sunnyslope Cemetery in Beaumont. Which Bogart residence is shown (the 1920s-built Beaumont home or another family property) is not confirmed, and the snowstorm is undated; heavy lowland snows recorded for inland Southern California include 11 Jan 1930, 15 Jan 1932 (called the heaviest on record in the LA Basin) and 9-11 Jan 1949.

img_a144edcec7a50be8.title: New Presbyterian Church under construction after a January snowstorm (701 Egan Ave), Beaumont
img_a144edcec7a50be8.description: A modern snapshot of a framed real-photo postcard (dark wood frame and window reflection visible): a masonry church under construction — coursed brick/block walls, tall arched windows with scaffolding visible through the openings, roof framing incomplete, a corner tower at left — amid trees bowed under heavy snow, with a mid-1910s touring car at the curb. The handwritten inscription reads 'Beaumont Calif. / The new Presbyterian Church unfinished(?) after snow storm Jan. 1[?]', with a later blue-ink year annotation most plausibly reading '1916'. The building is Beaumont's Presbyterian church at Seventh Street and Egan Avenue (701 Egan Ave) — not the congregation's later river-rock sanctuary at 7th & Euclid, which was built of Whitewater stone and completed 20 May 1934. When the rock church was finished, the Presbyterians sold the Egan Avenue building to the First Christian Church (1934), which still occupies it. The prior catalog date of c. 1930-1940 is therefore wrong: the church was 'new' and unfinished roughly two decades earlier, consistent with the automobile and the annotation.

img_b3dcb09d831e2058.title: Laura May Stewart with rifle and saddle in her ranch collection room
img_b3dcb09d831e2058.original_title: Laura May Stewart In The Room On Their Ranch Where She Collected Family Items
img_b3dcb09d831e2058.description: An elderly Laura May Stewart, in glasses and a checked dress, holds a rifle above a stock saddle; a coiled riata hangs on the wall at right and framed photographs of ranch and range scenes hang behind her — the room at the Stewart ranch where she gathered her family's pioneer relics. Stewart (c. 1885-1974) was one of five children of Reznor Perry Stewart and Mary Elizabeth Stewart, Pass pioneers whose 1883 homestead grew to more than 2,200 acres of Beaumont-Banning ranch land (today's Sun Lakes and Four Seasons areas), partly purchased from the Southern Pacific Railroad. Before her death in 1974 at age 89 she endowed the $1.2 million Laura May Stewart Trust, whose successor foundation still makes grants to Banning and Beaumont charities; the Trust is also the rights holder named on Stewart photographs in the Beaumont Library District's Calisphere collection. A halftone dot screen is clearly visible across this copy, showing it was re-photographed from a printed publication — most likely a local newspaper or history feature — which has not yet been identified.
